questions.question: A man in South Africa notices 2 ticks attached to his leg, then develops an eschar.
questions.question_raw: Q62 (2003 PM). Man in South Africa, notices 2 ticks attached to leg. Develops eschar

parts.text: What is the best way to make the diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: B) What is the best way to make the dx?

questions.model_answer: a) African tick-bite fever, caused by Rickettsia africae (sub-Saharan Africa, tick exposure, often multiple eschars). b) Diagnosis is primarily clinical/epidemiological. Best confirmatory test is PCR or immunohistochemistry on a swab or biopsy of the eschar (culture is difficult); serology by immunofluorescence is the reference method but seroconverts later and cross-reacts widely.

cohort_answer.text: A) African tick bite fever - Rickettsia africae. B) Diagnosis is clinical; skin bx for immunohistochemistry or PCR; can do serology (later).

questions.question: Name 1 rickettsial, 1 bacterial (non-rickettsial) and 1 viral cause of eschar and the clinical syndrome that each causes.

parts.text: Name 1 rickettsial, 1 bacterial (non-rickettsial) and 1 viral cause of eschar and the clinical syndrome that it causes.

parts_raw.text: Name 1 rickettsial, 1 bacterial (non-rickettsia) and 1 viral cause of eschar and the clinical syndrome that it causes.

questions.model_answer: (1) Rickettsial: Rickettsia africae - African tick-bite fever (fever, multiple inoculation eschars, regional lymphadenopathy). (2) Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Francisella tularensis - ulceroglandular tularaemia (cutaneous ulcer/eschar with tender regional lymphadenopathy). (3) Viral: Variola/orthopoxvirus (smallpox or vaccinia) - vesiculopustular lesions crusting into eschars.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the rickettsial cause is in this chapter (Table 185.3). Bacterial and viral eschar causes are from standard ID sources, not this chapter.

questions.question: A woman travels to Tanzania and climbs Mount Kilimanjaro. She presents with fever and an eschar. List 3 organisms on the differential.
questions.question_raw: A woman travels to Tanzania and climbs Mount Kilimanjaro. She presents with a fever and eschar.
questions.model_answer: (1) Rickettsia africae (African tick-bite fever) - the leading cause of fever with eschar in sub-Saharan Africa travelers; produces multiple inoculation eschars. (2) Francisella tularensis (ulceroglandular tularaemia) - eschar/ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy. (3) Bacillus anthracis (cutaneous anthrax) - painless black eschar. (Scrub typhus, Orientia tsutsugamushi, is an alternative but is not endemic to this region.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Only R. africae is grounded in this chapter (Table 185.3, sub-Saharan Africa, 100% multiple eschars); tularaemia and anthrax as eschar causes are from standard travel/ID sources (IDSA, CDC Yellow Book), not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: African trypanosomiasis; Tularemia; Rickettsia africae (African tick bite fever); Scrub typhus; Bacillus anthracis; Plague.

questions.question: List 1 infection (causative organism not required) under each category that causes an eschar.

parts_raw.text: List 1 infection (causative organism not required) under each category that cause an eschar - Rickettsial

questions.model_answer: a) Rickettsial: African tick-bite fever (Rickettsia africae) - alternatives include scrub typhus, Mediterranean spotted fever, rickettsialpox. b) Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Ulceroglandular tularaemia (Francisella tularensis); alternatively cutaneous anthrax or plague. c) Virus: Orthopoxvirus infection - smallpox/vaccinia (crusting eschar).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only part a) is grounded in this chapter (Table 185.3 lists rickettsioses with eschar). Bacterial and viral eschar causes are from standard ID sources, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Rickettsial: Scrub typhus, murine typhus, epidemic typhus, african tick bite fever (Orientia tsutsugamushi, rickettsia africae). Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Tularemia, plague (Francisella tularensis, yersinia pestis); Ecthyma (pseudomonas). Virus: Smallpox, vaccinia
